1.pericope_label: And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration. Then the twelve called the multitude of the disciples unto them, and said, It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables.

schools.summary: Ellicott holds that the English Grecians never means Greeks but Greek-speaking Jews of the dispersion, who read the Septuagint, as a rule neither read Hebrew nor spoke Aramaic, may by this date have outnumbered the Hebrews, and were more zealous for the holy places than the Jerusalem Jews familiar with them from infancy; he finds singular tact in the apostles' refusal either to resent the suspicion or to vindicate themselves, thinks they remembered how Moses delegated his authority, and hears in the action of the multitude the Greek sense of the word for assembly, where every citizen has his vote. Robertson keeps to the words, the murmuring being onomatopoetic for grumblings that buzz until they are heard, the multitude the whole church and not the hundred and twenty, and the tables those of the daily distribution of food rather than of money, from which he thinks the office of deacon grew, though he reports Furneaux as certain the seven are not the later deacons. Barnes answers why the office came so late, that while the church was small the apostles could distribute its alms themselves, and draws the rule that a church's temporal affairs should never be much entrusted to its clergy. Lightfoot observes that the rabbis were divided over whether Abraham was called a Hebrew from Heber or from having crossed the river.

Calvin reaches the same point as Barnes by the proverb that good laws take their beginning of evil manners: had deacons been proposed before the necessity appeared, the people would not have been ready, the apostles would have seemed to avoid labour, and many would not have given so liberally into other men's hands. He also finds patience in the apostles' not being more moved and prudence in their meeting the evil early, since a division grown strong is a wound hard to cure, and takes the meeting as proof that the church was governed by order. Gill counts the growth behind the trouble, from the hundred and twenty to three thousand and then five thousand.

Wesley makes the murmuring the first breach on a body that had been of one heart, asks how short a time pure Christianity remained in the world, and sees in this partiality the seeds of a general persecution, at once penal and medicinal; he also divides the work as the early church did, preaching the primary business of apostles and bishops and the care of the poor the secondary. Clarke agrees with Barnes that the phrase rendered not reason means not pleasing, the sense required being not fit or proper.

Henry is of two minds at once: it does the heart good to see the disciples multiplied, since opposition contributed to the gospel's success and this infant church multiplied, like the infant Jewish church in Egypt, the more it was afflicted, yet it casts a damp that the multiplying itself became the occasion of discord, when hitherto they had all been with one accord.

debates.question: Why was the office of deacon not created earlier?

positions.position: Because while the church was small the apostles could handle its alms themselves, and the need had to become manifest first
Because the people had to be convinced by experience, or they would have thought the apostles were dodging labour and given less freely

outliers.claim: Reads the multiplying of the disciples and the discord it caused as a single mixed providence, good and bad in the same breath

3.pericope_label: Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business. But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.

schools.summary: Barnes takes the right of selection to rest with the church and not the ministry, so that the apostles could never be charged with partiality or with embezzling what they administered, and calls the number seven merely convenient, denying that any church is bound to it now. Ellicott looks outside Judaism for the number, allowing the general reverence for seven but suggesting the Roman Hellenists, among whom a guild called the Seven Stewards arranged the banquets held for the gods, something like the later love-feasts, and had themselves been appointed to relieve the priests of a duty grown too heavy; on the qualifications he argues that the apostles plainly did not confine the Spirit's working to prophecy and tongues. Robertson notes that the better reading of the last clause is a future, we shall appoint, so the apostles' act follows the church's choice as a certainty. Lightfoot dissents about the electors, deriving the office from the synagogue with its three officers over the poor and supposing the seven were chosen out of the hundred and twenty, and by them only.

Gill infers from the versions that render the verb choose that deacons must belong to the church they serve and be chosen by the common suffrages of its people. Calvin puts it more sharply, that it is tyrannous for one man to make ministers at his pleasure, and complains that the deacons of Rome are left no office but handling the paten and chalice; on the apostles' own portion he hears in the verb the sense of being fastened to a thing, and warns pastors not to think their duty done because they have spent some time each day in teaching.

Clarke guesses that each of the seven took his day, so that the widows had a superintendent for every day of the week, takes the wisdom required to be prudence and economy since mere piety could not serve where so many had to be pleased, and calls the verb for continuing in prayer emphatic, adding that even apostles had no independent graces and that a minister who does not pray much studies in vain. Wesley agrees that it is no light matter to dispense even a church's temporal goods, wishes ministers in every age had acted as much in concert with their people, and calls the two duties the proper business of a bishop.

positions.position: The whole church, by common suffrage, the apostles only ratifying
Probably the hundred and twenty alone, and out of their own number

debates.question: Where does the number seven come from?

positions.position: Nowhere in particular: it is convenient, and no mystery attaches to it
Possibly from the Roman guild of Seven Stewards, themselves appointed to relieve the priests of a heavy duty
Perhaps from the seven good men of the city named by the rabbis, though he will not be curious about it

outliers.claim: Traces the number seven to a Roman collegium of stewards and makes it evidence for a Roman origin for Stephen himself

5.pericope_label: And the saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas a proselyte of Antioch: Whom they set before the apostles: and when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them. And the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly; and a great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.

schools.summary: Robertson calls the seven undoubtedly Hellenists and finds consummate wisdom in it, since the murmuring came from that side and seven of their own were now set over their widows, so that the trouble stayed settled; he also marks the imperfects of the closing verse keeping pace with one another and notes that the converted priests were usually Sadducees, a sad day for Annas and Caiaphas. Ellicott calls the inference from the Greek names natural but not necessary, allows that the Hebrews may have voted generously, suggests the order of names is the order of election with Stephen heading the poll, and connects the priests' conversion with Stephen's new teaching that the time for sacrifices had passed. Barnes names the Fathers who derive the Nicolaitans from Nicolas and answers that the evidence is not clear. Lightfoot dissents from the whole Hellenist reading, preferring to call the seven Hebrews who understood Greek, since it is hardly supposable that Stephen pleaded before the Sanhedrin in a tongue not his own, and notes that the rabbis made synagogue officers with a form of words and no imposition of hands.

Calvin will not let faith be separated from the Spirit, as though faith were not itself the Spirit's gift, and takes the Spirit here for Stephen's other graces, zeal, wisdom, uprightness and integrity of conscience, the rest of the seven being less commended as inferior to him; he reports the ancient consent that Nicolas is the man of the Revelation and draws from it that we must not be negligent in choosing ministers, holds that the laying on of hands has of itself no force since the effect depends on the Spirit alone, and distinguishes the two ways the word of God grows, restraining this increase to Jerusalem. Gill reads the episode as a stratagem of Satan that failed, issuing in better discipline and a wider spread of the gospel.

Clarke reports both sides of the Nicolas question, adding that Clement of Alexandria gives him a good character and that he is the only proselyte listed, the rest being taken for native Jews; on the converted priests he calls it one of the greatest miracles of grace and draws from it that sinners are converted not by miracles but by the preaching of Christ crucified. Wesley agrees the seven were Hellenists, thinks the proselyte was chosen because proselytes would more readily apply to him, and says simply of the growth that the hindrances were removed.

Leo, preaching on the martyrs, sets the matter under the love of God and neighbour, in which the martyrs stand nearest to the Lord in imitation as in likeness of suffering; and though no man's kindness can equal the love that redeemed us, they did great service in showing that death and the cross need not be terrible to any follower.

debates.question: Were the seven Hellenists or Hebrews?

positions.position: Hellenists, as their Greek names show, and deliberately chosen from the aggrieved party
Hebrews who understood Greek, which is why the Hellenists' widows were committed to them

debates.question: Did the Nicolaitans take their name from this Nicolas?

positions.position: Yes, on the great consent of the ancient writers
The Fathers say so but the evidence is not clear
No: the name more likely comes from a phrase meaning let us eat together

outliers.claim: Leaves the exegesis entirely and preaches the martyrs, setting Stephen's appointment under the love of God and neighbour before any of his story has been told

8.pericope_label: And Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people. Then there arose certain of the synagogue, which is called the synagogue of the Libertines, and Cyrenians, and Alexandrians, and of them of Cilicia and of Asia, disputing with Stephen. And they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake.

schools.summary: Ellicott and Robertson both report that the better manuscripts read grace rather than faith, Robertson finding in the four words a picture of remarkable attractiveness; Robertson keeps the imperfect of the disputing, that they continued to have no strength to take a stand, and pictures Stephen knocking them down, Saul included, as fast as they got up, while Ellicott finds it remarkable that Stephen is the first Christian teacher of whom wisdom is specially predicated, a word the Gospels reserve for our Lord. On the synagogue Ellicott separates Libertines, Cyrenians and Alexandrians from the men of Cilicia and Asia, takes the Libertini for emancipated Roman Jews descended from Pompey's captives, and thinks Stephen sprang from them; Robertson allows either two groups or five and says plainly that Luke's language is not clear. Barnes repeats the common estimate of four hundred and eighty synagogues in the city, and denies that the spirit Stephen spoke with means the Holy Spirit, making it his own energy and ardour, since evident sincerity convinces men further than the ablest argument delivered coldly.

Calvin calls this a new combat, the church assaulted in the person of one man, and traces the shape of persecution: the wicked first assault the gospel with the tongue, and only when disputing fails do they fly to slander and tumult and at last to violence. He also cautions against pressing the word full, since we are not to imagine perfection of faith, Scripture commonly calling those full of God's gifts who are abundantly endued with them, and supposes that Roman freedmen built the synagogue at their own charge for Jews arriving from the provinces. Gill takes the power to mean at once the power to preach, to defend the gospel, to bear indignities and to work miracles, and notes that one ancient copy adds the words which was in him.

Clarke reports how many versions carry the reading grace and that some copies join both, prefers Bishop Pearce's solution that the Libertines should be looked for in Libya beside the Cyrenians and Alexandrians rather than at Rome, and holds against Barnes that the spirit Stephen spoke with was the Holy Spirit and its power irresistible, so that his hearers must either yield to its teaching or be confounded by its truth. Wesley makes the synagogue a single one serving all these nations and guesses that Saul of Cilicia belonged to it and perhaps Gamaliel presided over it.

Henry makes the fullness an argument, that those full of faith are full of power because by faith the power of God is engaged for us, and that Stephen's faith so filled him it left no room for unbelief; he adds that Stephen had not thought the office of distributing charity beneath him, and being faithful in a little was entrusted with more.

Chrysostom sees the promotion differently from the rest: even among the seven one was pre-eminent and won the first prize, drawing greater grace upon himself though the ordination was common to them all, and he observes that Stephen worked no signs until he became publicly known, which shows that grace alone is not sufficient but that there must be ordination too, a further access of the Spirit beyond what came by baptism.

From Libya, beside the Cyrenians and Alexandrians, rather than from Rome at all
One synagogue serving all the nations named

11.pericope_label: Then they suborned men, which said, We have heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses, and against God. And they stirred up the people, and the elders, and the scribes, and came upon him, and caught him, and brought him to the council, And set up false witnesses, which said, This man ceaseth not to speak blasphemous words against this holy place, and the law: For we have heard him say, that this Jesus of Nazareth shall destroy this place, and shall change the customs which Moses delivered us. And all that sat in the council, looking stedfastly on him, saw his face as it had been the face of an angel.

schools.summary: Barnes defines suborning as procuring a man to swear falsely and explains the method, not open falsehood but the perverting of Stephen's doctrine and the putting forward of their own inferences as what he had maintained, which he calls the common way of opposing a doctrine one dislikes; he asks why the witnesses are called false if they only reported what Stephen said and answers that they perverted his meaning, doubting he ever used those words. Robertson notes what the charge reveals, Moses standing before God in it and practically on a par, and that blasphemy was punished by stoning; he says they shook the people together like an earthquake, calls it the first record of the masses turning hostile to the disciples, and grants that Stephen had caught the spirit of what Jesus said at the well, that God is spirit and may be worshipped anywhere. Ellicott holds the accusation false but its falsehood a distortion of truth, each count resting on words really spoken, reconstructs from it that Stephen taught the Temple's days were numbered and the Law was to give way to a higher revelation, and takes the customs for the whole system of the Law. Lightfoot reads the shining face as God's own verdict, bearing witness by a miracle that Stephen had done Moses no wrong.

Calvin reads the turn to witnesses as a defeat confessed: overcome by the power of the Spirit they give over disputing and fall back on slander, striving against their own conscience, since nothing is more unfitting than to rest a cause upon lies, and even a guilty man must not be borne down by false testimony, though hypocrites who shroud themselves in zeal give themselves leave. On the face he keeps sober, taking it not of Stephen's natural features but of his bearing at that moment, for where the arraigned are commonly pale and stammering, in Stephen there appeared a certain majesty. Gill explains why the people were so easily wrought on, nothing provoking them like a hint that the rites of Moses were slighted.

Clarke says they made underhand work with profligates who for money would swear anything, is bitterest at the elders and scribes making themselves one with the basest of the people and bringing a good man before a council ready for every evil work, and thinks they had likely heard Stephen say something to that effect, true enough in the spirit from which it came, but gave it a false colouring; on the shining face he fills in the rabbinic background, where God distinguishes eminent men by a glory in the face, one writer describing Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh with faces like the sun and words like thunder. Wesley puts the whole difficulty shortest, that so they might have heard him, but the consequence they drew would not follow.

debates.question: In what sense were the witnesses false?

They had likely heard something of the kind and gave true words a false colouring

outliers.claim: Asks where Peter and John were at the crisis, observing that Stephen stands before the council alone as Jesus had, with no Gamaliel to interpose this time
